papers.title: Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors with a high migration-to-proliferation ratio (D/k) are associated with treatment resistance, motivating the estimation of D/k from routine pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and the investigation of mechanisms underlying its heterogeneity across patients. Unlike previous approaches based on nested spherical approximations of enhancing and non-enhancing tumor volumes, we incorporate the spatial arrangement of the enhancing and non-enhancing tumor regions by deriving a 1D tumor density distribution from their segmentations and fitting a 1D reaction-diffusion model to estimate D/k. We achieved an error of under 5% when comparing our method to synthetic density distributions and found excellent correlation with synthetic tumor segmentations (Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.996). We then evaluated associations between patient-specific D/k values and their clinical, transcriptomic, and radiomic features. When applied to 102 pre-treatment MRI scans from the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2017 dataset, elevated D/k significantly correlated with reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.01), older age (p = 0.04), and a trend toward lower Karnofsky Performance Status (p = 0.059). In a subset of 91 patients with available microarray data, mesenchymal-like phenotypes consistently exhibited elevated D/k across three established molecular subtype classifications (p = 0.013, p = 0.055, and p = 0.127). Elastic Net regularization followed by overrepresentation analysis revealed an enrichment of glycosylation-related pathways among genes associated with D/k variability (p = 0.0123 and p = 0.0368). Furthermore, Multi-Omic Factor Analysis identified a radiomic factor correlated with D/k (r = 0.57, p = 4x10-9), with the highest-weighted features corresponding to smoothness of the non-enhancing tumor region on T2 and FLAIR.

papers.title: Distinct labeling of host and viral genomes highlights redistribution of nuclear proteins during HSV-1 infection
papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) coordinates viral and cellular proteins during infection. While proteins associated with HSV-1 genomes have been identified, changes in proteins associated with the host genome during infection remain poorly understood. We adapted accelerated native isolation of proteins on nascent DNA (aniPOND) to label and purify cellular and viral DNA then identify associated proteins by mass spectrometry. Using this approach, we confirm observations that cellular transcription, DNA replication, and repair proteins are enriched on viral genomes after the onset of viral DNA replication. We assessed how protein interactions with cellular DNA change during infection relative to protein abundance. Targets of the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase, ICP0, are depleted from the nucleus and cellular genome during infection. Transcription regulatory factors, Pol II, and the proteasome are depleted from the host genome, while association with DNA damage response and nuclear pore proteins increases. We also provide evidence for HSV-1 disruption of ribosome biogenesis. Results demonstrate reorganization of the nucleus during infection and validate this technique to identify changes to host genome-associated factors during infection.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of Helicobacter pylori infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen
papers.abstract: Background. Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories. Methods. NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of H. pylori-infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales. Results. Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR 1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5x10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions. Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.

papers.title: Systematic analysis reveals an Mln1-dependent trade-off between metabolic flexibility and thermotolerance in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: During infection, fungal pathogens must adapt to multiple environmental challenges, including changes in temperature, nutrient availability, and immune stress. Although transcriptional regulators are central to these adaptations, how individual regulators contribute to distinct environmental responses and how these responses are functionally interconnected remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functions of infection-associated transcription factors under distinct host-relevant conditions in Cryptococcus neoformans. Integrating in vivo expression profiling with infectivity data from signature-tagged mutagenesis, we prioritized 24 transcription factors, 12 of which were induced under host-mimicking conditions. Initial functional analyses revealed distinct roles for these transcription factors in adaptation to temperature, carbon, and nitrogen availability. Further characterization of Mln1, a fungal basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, uncovered an unexpected connection between carbon source adaptation and thermotolerance. Mig1-dependent repression limited MLN1 expression in the presence of glucose, whereas Mln1 accumulated in the nucleus in the presence of trehalose or ethanol, but not glucose. Loss of MLN1 impaired carbon-starvation gene expression and growth on non-preferred carbon sources, particularly trehalose. Conversely, mln1{Delta} cells accumulated more intracellular trehalose and exhibited enhanced thermotolerance, yet showed reduced melanization, titan cell formation, virulence in Drosophila, and brain fungal burden in mice. Together, these results suggest that Mln1 contributes to metabolic flexibility and fungal virulence while differentially influencing thermotolerance. More broadly, these findings highlight a potential physiological trade-off between nutrient utilization and stress resistance, suggesting that these adaptive processes may be interconnected in fungal pathogens.

papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: DGM Is Dead; Long Live DGM-Star! A Quantization-Theoretic Approach to Gamma Rate Discretization
papers.abstract: Modeling substitution rate heterogeneity as a discretized Gamma distribution is standard in phylogenetic inference. Ferretti et al. (2026) have recently demonstrated that the most commonly used equiprobable Gamma rate discretization, known simply as the discrete Gamma model (DGM), substantially overestimates average branch lengths in reconstructed phylogenies when the true rates are drawn from a continuous Gamma distribution. We propose an alternative method to discretize the Gamma rate distribution that considerably reduces the bias in estimated branch lengths and can be used as a drop-in replacement for the standard DGM. The method works especially well on large trees with short branches, yielding up to a 20-fold reduction in bias on simulated phylogenies. It is developed by applying quantization-theoretic tools to the analysis of a simplified star-phylogeny abstraction introduced by Ferretti et al. (2026), where the new method is unbiased by construction. We explain Ferretti et al.'s counterintuitive observation that increasing the number of rate categories can exacerbate the bias of the standard DGM, even though this should in principle make DGM a better approximation to the continuous case, and offer our method as an immediately available alternative.

papers.title: Joint QTL mapping reveals patterns of pleiotropy across structured environments in budding yeast
papers.abstract: Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies in model organisms have long been used to infer the structure of genotype-phenotype maps. However, prior work has largely focused on analyzing the genetic architecture of complex traits individually. Here, we sought to instead infer genotype-phenotype maps for a large set of related phenotypes simultaneously. To do so, we used bulk assays to measure the competitive fitness of each of 100,000 individuals from a large budding yeast QTL mapping panel across a set of 101 phenotypes related by a ``hub-and-perturbation'' pattern, and then used a forward search approach to jointly infer the genetic basis of all phenotypes together. Our results reveal complex patterns of pleiotropy in the genetic architecture of these traits. We find that these patterns of pleiotropy reflect the structure of the environmental relationships as well as functional information about individual variants and the interactions between them. This suggests that high-throughput QTL mapping across structured environments can help uncover biologically meaningful genetic interactions, along with their variation across related environmental contexts.

papers.title: SF3b inhibitors suppress proliferation of nonsmall cell lung cancer cells irrespective of EGFR mutation status
papers.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard care for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance limits their durability, and alternatives that do not depend on EGFR kinase activity are needed. We asked whether inhibitors of SF3b, a core component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle, act on NSCLC cells regardless of EGFR genotype. Three lung adenocarcinoma lines were treated with pladienolide B or herboxidiene at 0.01, 0.1 and 1 uM: PC9 and HCC827, both carrying an EGFR exon 19 deletion and both inhibited by gefitinib at nanomolar concentrations, and A549, which is EGFR wild type and gefitinibin sensitive. Proliferation was followed for three days by crystal violet staining, EGFR intron 2 retention was assayed by RTPCR, and EGFR protein was measured by western blotting. Both compounds produced a concentration-dependent increase in the intron 2 retained product in all three lines, and both held proliferation at or near the day 0 cell number in all three, at concentrations down to 0.01 uM. EGFR protein was lost in PC9, reduced in A549, and only partly reduced in HCC827, where a residual band persisted in lanes whose growth was fully suppressed. Since A549 is EGFR wild-type, and published knockdown data show that removing EGFR does not suppress proliferation of wild-type lines, the growth inhibition cannot be attributed to loss of EGFR alone. We read EGFR intron 2 retention as a marker of target engagement rather than as the mechanism of the growth effect. These are the results of single experiments without replicates or statistical testing and should be read as preliminary.

papers.title: Shared and Specific miRNA-mRNA in Human and Murine Acute Kidney Injury
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is managed as a single clinical entity despite substantial biological heterogeneity. We established a cross-species framework to define etiology-specific molecular programs and determine how these programs relate to molecular heterogeneity and pathobiology in human AKI. We performed parallel sequencing of totalRNA (mRNA) and miRNA (kidney, whole blood) in 3 murine models (mild AKI: ischemia-reperfusion injury, IRI; cecal-ligation and puncture, CLP; endotoxemia, LPS); kidney mRNA and miRNA clearly distinguished the models, blood mRNA maintained model-specific separation, and blood miRNA was less distinct. IRI was characterized by epithelial injury/repair, and extracellular matrix remodeling (i.e., miR-125b-1-3p, Vim, Sprr2g); CLP, broader inflammatory, metabolic programs (i.e., miR-692, Pfkfb3, Cdo1); LPS, inflammatory signaling (i.e., miR-155-5p, Irf7, Gbp3). We then compared these signatures to human whole blood RNAseq. Human blood samples varied along a shared gene axis that correlated to differing degrees with all three murine models, consistent with the heterogeneous nature of clinical AKI rather than discrete assignment to a single experimental etiology. Orthologs were linked to immune processes (i.e., SIGLEC14, DAAM2, CD177, DEFA3), and the presence of tubular casts in human biopsies, reflecting that mild murine AKI models capture etiology-specific biology relevant to severe human AKI. Integration of injury etiology, severity, and time may provide a framework for developing circulating biomarkers that may resolve the biological heterogeneity of human AKI.

papers.title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
papers.abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

papers.title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
papers.abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

papers.title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium
papers.abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.

papers.title: YhdP forms an envelope-spanning phospholipid-binding bridge in complex with DedD
papers.abstract: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is built from phospholipids synthesised at the inner membrane, but how they cross the periplasm remains unresolved. YhdP is the leading candidate for anterograde phospholipid transfer and is predicted to form an envelope-spanning bridge. Here we purify YhdP at endogenous levels and show by cryo-electron microscopy that it contains a continuous cavity, alongside an additional density that proteomics identifies as the cell wall-binding protein DedD. Liposome co-sedimentation shows that the C-terminal helices of YhdP bind membranes directly, and single-molecule tracking reveals that endogenous YhdP is as immobile as an outer membrane protein, indicating an envelope-spanning architecture in vivo. Native mass spectrometry demonstrates that the YhdP groove accommodates all major classes of E. coli phospholipid without headgroup preference. DedD engages YhdP through its disordered region and increases lipid density at the groove entrance, suggesting a potential role in lipid loading.

papers.title: The large conjugative plasmid pAB3 integrates into the chromosome of Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 17978
papers.abstract: ATCC 17978 is one of the most utilised lab strains of Acinetobacter baumannii. Current literature suggests ATCC 17978 can have either a sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype or have the type VI secretion system (T6SS) switched on depending on the presence/absence of the large conjugative plasmid pAB3, which encodes the antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) sul2 and T6SS repressors tetR1/tetR2. Here, we show that pAB3 integrates into the ATCC 17978 chromosome, which enables a large inversion resulting in the chromosomal arrangement labelled GS2.24 by Socru. This integration has no transcriptional impact on nearby genes or tetR1/tetR2. We find several instances were a portion of integrated pAB3 containing tetR2 is lost but the rest of the sequence, including sul2, is maintained, suggesting pAB3 integration may serve to make further rearrangements more tractable, enabling a putative T6SS+ sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype.

papers.title: Lipopolysaccharide and Wzi retain capsular polysaccharide at the Klebsiella pneumoniae cell surface and promote bloodstream infection fitness
papers.abstract: Bacterial capsules are formed by individual capsular polysaccharide (CPS) polymers and are the outermost extracellular layers of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Capsules affect several aspects of bacterial biology, including resistance to host immune factors, survival in unfavorable environments and antimicrobial resistance. Research on CPS biology has largely focused on its synthesis and the pathogenic consequences of its presence or absence. Beyond synthesis, our understanding of its retention (attachment) on the cell surface is limited. Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important Gram-negative pathogen and expresses more than 80 capsular serotypes using the common Wzy-dependent CPS biosynthesis system and phenotypically manifests in various forms, making this species an attractive bacterial model to study the underexplored aspects of CPS biology. Here, we identified and characterized bacterial components involved in CPS retention in K. pneumoniae and assessed the importance of CPS retention on bloodstream fitness. Our examination revealed that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the outer-membrane protein, Wzi, collectively retain K. pneumoniae CPS on the bacterial surface. We demonstrate that the core-oligosaccharide domain of LPS and the extracellular surface of Wzi likely provide anchoring sites for CPS on the bacterial surface. Furthermore, CPS retention depends on divalent cation availability. Importantly, CPS retention on the bacterial surface is important for survival in serum and bacterial fitness at secondary infection sites in a murine bacteremia model. Together, our findings demonstrate that the functional importance of CPS to bacteria extends beyond synthesis and its overall abundance. Bacterial control over other CPS properties, like cell surface retention, are also important for K. pneumoniae fitness during bacteremia.

papers.title: How to stand out to a mate - Flash colour of Photinus fireflies maximizes signal contrast against ambient light
papers.abstract: During twilight, flying male Photinus fireflies flash in search for conspecific females, which sit on the vegetation below and flash back in response. However, before darkness sets in, the green vegetation in the habitat makes the detection of flashes more difficult. Twilight active fireflies tend to emit more yellow flashes than nocturnal fireflies and it has been proposed that firefly flash colour evolved to enhance the contrast of firefly flashes against their signalling background. There is indirect evidence for this contrast hypothesis, but it remains to be rigorously tested. This is the first study to directly test the contrast hypothesis by recording ambient light spectra in three different habitats throughout the daily flash activity of Photinus pyralis and P. australis and comparing these ambient light spectra to the male flash spectra of the two species. The contrast hypothesis predicts that during peak activity, firefly light colour will maximally contrast with the signalling background. Our data show that male flash spectra fit into a gap in the ambient light spectrum that opens during peak flashing activity of each species, effectively enhancing the visual contrast between male flashes and their background and making males more visible to their potential mates.

papers.title: Variational quantum thermalization of environment-coupled DNA sequence biases
papers.abstract: Understanding whether environmental conditions bias the statistical weight of specific genomic configurations requires a framework connecting molecular interactions, thermal fluctuations, and sequence-level observables. Here, we model DNA as an open quantum system coupled to an environmental thermal bath (represented as an external bosonic field) and parameterize the underlying molecular interaction energies (effective Hamiltonian terms) directly from prescribed nucleotide sequences. To evaluate sequence distributions at thermodynamic equilibrium, we compare two finite-temperature strategies at fixed inverse temperature ($beta=1$): classical Bayesian optimization targeting the exact thermodynamic equilibrium distribution (the Gibbs state), and quantum simulation using a Variational Quantum Thermalizer (VQT) implemented via a nine-layer parameterized quantum circuit. Both methods optimize the same interaction energy model and target-sequence objective across short oligomers ($N=2$--$5$ base pairs), using 200 outer evaluations. Benchmarking against a uniform sequence distribution, exact-Gibbs optimization enhances target-sequence probabilities by factors of $9.11$, $25.64$, $54.51$, and $159.87$. The VQT approach similarly yields substantial target enrichment across all sequence lengths, achieving enhancement factors between $9.85$ and $62.77$. By evaluating the VQT-selected Hamiltonians against exact Gibbs calculations, we decouple optimization errors in parameter learning from approximation errors inherent to the variational quantum circuit. While concordance with the exact-Gibbs optimum is high in shorter oligomers, larger systems exhibit heightened sensitivity to variational thermal approximations. These results demonstrate that environment-induced sequence biases can be systematically captured within a variational quantum simulation framework, bridging biophysical models of DNA thermodynamics with quantum algorithms for finite-temperature state preparation. Crucially, the resulting equilibrium probabilities represent intrinsic thermodynamic biases rather than realized evolutionary substitution rates, which remain governed by kinetic activation barriers, replication fidelity, and enzymatic DNA repair.

papers.title: Dairy cattle movement networks govern the spread and persistence of H5N1 B3.13 in the United States
papers.abstract: Avian influenza virus H5N1 is predominantly found in wild and domestic birds. H5N1 genotype B3.13 was first detected in United States dairy cattle in March 2024 and spread through much of the country during 2024 and 2025, resulting in the largest known H5N1 outbreak in domestic mammals. By analysing viral genomic data jointly with historical cattle movement patterns, we find that live cattle movement is the predominant contributor to H5N1 spatial spread, rather than wild or domestic birds. Using phylogeographic methods we estimate that >40% of interstate viral transmissions occurred before B3.13's first detection and >70% occurred before interstate dairy cattle movement restrictions were implemented in April 2024. After this implementation, interstate transmission slowed but within-state spread persisted, driven by local cattle network density and movement volume. Our epidemic simulations demonstrate that the connectivity of counties within and around the Texas Panhandle - where the earliest cases were documented - predisposed the region to become an outbreak epicentre. Counterfactual simulations indicate that interstate restrictions needed to have begun 2-3 months earlier in order to limit the epizootic substantively, given the extent of cryptic spread before detection. Network-informed interventions outperformed geographically-defined containment, but response speed (rather than intervention strength) was the limiting factor in our epidemic models, underscoring the need for surveillance systems capable of detecting pathogen emergence before widespread dissemination.

papers.title: Termite-Like Phylogenetic Conservation of Gut Microbiota in Passalid Beetles Suggests Evolutionary Convergence in Decaying Wood Degradation
papers.abstract: Beetles of the family Passalidae are an important group of subsocial wood-decomposing (saproxylophagous) insects, spending their entire life cycle living inside and feeding on rotten logs. Decaying wood is an abundant resource, but nutritionally poor and challenging to digest. As in other saproxylophagous insects, digestion for passalids is only possible through symbiotic relationships with their gut microbiota, highlighting the critical roles of these symbionts in the evolution of wood-decomposing insects. Despite its importance, this critical symbiotic relationship remains poorly understood, hindering our ability to identify the factors shaping this association and assessing its role in the evolution of Passalidae. Using high-throughput sequencing of the microbial 16S rRNA we comparatively analyzed the composition and abundance of symbiont lineages in the anterior hindguts of passalid beetles from two independent mountain systems in the Colombian Caribbean region. We tested the influence of geographical co-occurrence and phylogenetic relatedness on gut microbial composition and structure. We posit that if shared locality was the primary driver of gut microbiome assembly, then sympatric species should harbor more similar microbiomes regardless of their phylogenetic relationships. Alternatively, if host evolutionary history is the dominant factor, congeneric species should exhibit more similar microbiomes regardless of geographic co-occurrence. Our results support that phylogenetic relatedness explained substantially more variation in both bacterial and archaeal communities than geographic locality, indicating that gut microbiome composition is primarily structured by host evolutionary history. Furthermore, bacterial and archaeal communities exhibited evidence of phylosymbiosis, although at different phylogenetic scales: bacterial communities more closely reflected relationships among genus level clades, whereas archaeal communities retained congruence mainly at deeper host lineages. We also uncovered extensive bacterial taxonomic novelty, with nearly half of bacterial reads remaining unclassified at the genus level, highlighting the large undescribed microbial diversity associated with Passalidae. These findings lead to establishing Passalidae as a promising comparative model for investigating the evolutionary processes governing gut microbiome assembly and the evolution of lignocellulose-feeding symbioses.

papers.title: Proteomics reveals conserved features of histone biology in dinoflagellates
papers.abstract: Current knowledge of DNA packaging in eukaryotic nuclei largely centers on its basic unit, the nucleosome. Multiple lineages have, however, diverged from this paradigm, most notably dinoflagellates. Among other molecular oddities, these enigmatic protists have enormous genomes, permanently condensed chromosomes and a foreign gene encoding Dinoflagellate Viral Nucleoprotein (DVNP), which is used for packing DNA. Some dinoflagellates also have Histone-like Proteins (HLPs) acquired from bacteria via lateral gene transfer. Dinoflagellates were long thought to lack histones entirely, but canonical histone genes have been identified by transcriptomics. Here, we performed proteomics on purified nuclei and confirmed the presence of all four core histone classes, along with variants, and DVNP in the dinoflagellates Oxyrrhis marina and Amphidinium carterae and HLPs in A. carterae. We also identified putative histone post-translational modifications found in canonical eukaryotes. Comparative genomics of dinoflagellates revealed histone-handling and modification machinery alongside an apparent reduction in, or diversification of, machinery responsible for replication-dependent nucleosome deposition (CAF-1), consistent with a predominantly transcription-associated role for nucleosomes. Furthermore, proteomics revealed modifications of DVNP and HLP, raising the possibility of machinery co-opting. These observations support a new model of a dinoflagellate chromatin that includes the localization of canonical nucleosomes to insulated chromatin territories (INTs).

papers.title: Speciation, sexual selection, and the macroevolution of cricket mating signals
papers.abstract: Animal mating signals can communicate both species-specific recognition information and male phenotypic quality persuasion information to females. Using a comparative framework across an entire clade, we show that mating signal traits specifically associated with conspecific signal recognition show fast initial divergence during speciation, followed by relative stasis at equilibrium, and that this effect is enhanced among species pairs with the potential for gene flow. In contrast, sexually selected persuasion mating signal evolution is not associated with initial species divergence. These results reveal mechanistically how and when rapid mating signal evolution facilitates speciation and challenge the prevailing view that traits experiencing intrapopulation sexual selection are likely to be the major traits which promote interspecific divergence. In particular, the results suggest that the mechanistic link between sexual selection and speciation is ephemeral. We expect that the distinction between recognition and persuasion traits, and the particular importance of divergence in recognition traits for speciation, should be a widespread phenomenon.

papers.title: MC1R residue 223 is a convergent target for coat-colour lightening in domestic and wild bovids
papers.abstract: Whether similar phenotypes evolve through shared substitutions or alternative molecular routes is a central question in evolutionary genomics. Grey-coated taurine cattle provide a powerful system for investigating this question using geographically distinct Podolian and Alpine lineages. We combined whole-genome resequencing data, complementary selection scans (hapFLK, DCMS and FST) and contrasts between grey-coated and non-grey-coated breeds to investigate the molecular evolution of grey coat colour. Selection analyses identified candidate regions associated with Podolian/steppe divergence and a prominent pigmentation-related signal on BTA18 contaning FANCA, MC1R, and SPIRE2. Most grey breeds shared a BTA18 haplotype containing MC1R p.Arg223Trp and additional candidate variants. Tyrolean Grey cattle lacked this predominant haplotype but carried the coding duplication p.Gly220_Arg223dup, together with differentiation near the ASIP regulatory region. Thus, different candidate coding changes affect the same MC1R residue in different cattle lineages. Haplotype comparisons supported independent Podolian and Alpine origins for p.Arg223Trp and p.Gly220_Arg223dup insertion, respectively. Ancient-genome screening yielded no validated evidence of either variant except p.Arg223Trp in medieval cattle. Comparisons across 1,108 mammalian taxa identified independent recurrence of p.Arg223Trp in the white-coated mountain goat, Oreamnos americanus, where the derived allele was fixed in surveyed individuals (JTT-based neutral probability = 0.0043). Our findings support a model in which grey coat colour in cattle evolved through at least two partially distinct molecular routes within interacting pigmentation pathways. More broadly, they identify MC1R residue 223 as a candidate recurrent target of coat-colour lightening and illustrate how domesticated and wild lineages can repeatedly target constrained functional positions during phenotypic evolution.

papers.title: H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds
papers.abstract: In November 2025, the first global H5N5 infection was reported in a person in Washington State. Previously, these viruses had only been detected in seabirds and shorebirds near the Atlantic Ocean, suggesting potentially distinct ecology from dominant H5N1 strains. Using 354 global H5N5 genomes, we show that H5N5 viruses have been carried by high latitude seabirds and shorebirds across the Atlantic at least 9 times, with introductions more frequent in the fall and spring. We reconstruct a plausible path of cross-continental movement via Arctic or sub-Arctic regions, followed by a year of cryptic circulation prior to human spillover. These data show that H5N5 viruses have undergone far more intercontinental movements than previously recognized, and exhibit host and geographic patterns that are fundamentally distinct from dominant H5N1 lineages. The distinct host ecology, geography, and movement, paired with the capacity to infect a person, suggest that enhanced surveillance may be warranted.

papers.title: Diversity-generating retroelements enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.
papers.abstract: Diversity-generating retroelements (DGRs) are genetic elements that use error-prone reverse transcription to hypermutate specific target genes, most often the receptor-binding proteins of phages. They are enriched in human gut viruses, where they are hypothesised to enable phages expand their host range. Yet DGR-mediated host-range expansion across bacterial species has so far only been predicted in silico and has not been examined directly within complex microbial communities. To test this hypothesis in situ, we tracked phage-host interactions in the human gut, combining bulk metagenomic, virus-like particle (VLP), and Hi-C sequencing of longitudinal faecal samples collected over a five-week period. This culture-independent approach identified 380 interactions between 97 phages and 76 bacterial hosts. Nearly a third of these phages (31 of 97) encoded a DGR, and DGR-encoding phages were more likely to interact with multiple bacterial species. Moreover, nucleotide diversity in DGR-targeted genes increased with the number of hosts a phage interacted with and was concentrated in the surface-exposed, DGR-targeted variable region of its receptor-binding proteins. Together, these results provide in situ evidence that DGRs enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.

papers.title: A genomic baseline for long-term monitoring of economically important aquatic species in the Netherlands
papers.abstract: Aquatic species of economic and ecological importance are increasingly threatened by environmental change, yet their genetic diversity and population structure remain poorly characterised, limiting effective conservation and management. To address this gap, we initiated a multi-species genomic monitoring programme in 2022, targeting key marine and freshwater taxa. A total of 2,420 individuals from 104 locations were sampled across six species: turbot (Scophthalmus maximus), zander (Sander lucioperca), European eel (Anguilla anguilla; both glass eel in the marine environment and adult eel in freshwater environments), blue mussel (Mytilus edulis), flat oyster (Ostrea edulis), and Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas). Using genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) and SNP arrays, we generated genome-wide SNP datasets to assess population structure, genetic diversity, inbreeding, and relatedness. Among fish species, population structure was generally weak, consistent with high connectivity. However, significant variation in genetic diversity and kinship among localities indicates the presence of distinct source populations that may be critical for maintaining adaptive potential and guiding restoration efforts. In bivalves, cultured populations in the Oosterschelde and Waddenzee were genetically homogeneous, whereas wild populations in Grevelingen and Veerse Meer retained distinct genetic signatures, representing important reservoirs of diversity for conservation and breeding. Together, these results provide a genomic baseline for key aquatic species in the Netherlands and demonstrate the value of coordinated, multi-species genomic monitoring. The identification of genetically distinct and diverse populations offers direct guidance for conservation prioritisation, restoration strategies, and the sustainable management of aquatic genetic resources under ongoing environmental change, in the Netherlands but also applied in other national and transnational monitoring contexts.

papers.title: Pre-existing genome architecture partitions viral takeover in the smallest free-living eukaryote
papers.abstract: Nuclear DNA viruses colonize host genomes already structured into complex spatial domains, yet whether established spatial boundaries dictate viral progression remains unresolved--in part because sequence composition and transcriptional output are intertwined in animal models. Here, we tracked productive lytic infection of the marine picoeukaryote Ostreococcus tauri by the giant double-stranded DNA prasinovirus OtV5, recording transcription, accessibility, and 3D contact dynamics across parallel time courses. Although total cellular transcript pools collapsed 18-fold by 10 h post-infection, the host transcriptional shutdown, decay of insulation, early chromatin opening, and viral DNA positioning were all bounded by architectural coordinates defined prior to viral arrival. Across two low-GC outlier domains, chromatin accessibility spiked rapidly, spatial insulation eroded, and loci exhibited relative upregulation by 6 hpi, with the smaller outlier region retaining elevated transcript levels per cell compared to the rest of the genome. Unexpectedly, viral DNA was preferentially depleted from these accessible outlier cores, contacting instead the standard-GC telomeric flanks situated immediately beyond the pre-existing spatial boundaries. Domain identity, rather than local accessibility or active host expression, thus governs viral positioning, demonstrating that pre-existing nuclear architecture partitions the physical and transcriptional takeover of the host cell.

papers.title: An integrated identifiability and metabolic flux analysis workflow for reducing and repairing dynamic CHO metabolic models
papers.abstract: Over-parametrized kinetic-metabolic models can fit available data accurately yet still yield unreliable parameter estimates and output uncertainties. We developed an integrated workflow that combines Fisher information matrix-based identifiability analysis diagnostics, uncertainty propagation, and metabolic flux analysis (MFA) to reduce model size and assess the transferability of a kinetically constrained dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) model of CHO perfusion culture. Using Control medium data, the dFBA model size was reduced from 48 to 43 kinetic parameters while maintaining performance across 23 measured extracellular species. The reduced models transferability was assessed by predicting cell behavior in an amino acid-supplemented medium (Medium C), which lowered the specific growth rate while increasing specific productivity. The reduced model successfully predicted viable cell density, antibody titer, and supplemented amino acids for Medium C but failed to capture the reversal of glutamate metabolism and the increase in lactate production. Output uncertainty quantification identified structural gaps rather than parameter uncertainty as the underlying cause of prediction failures, with 79% of Medium C experimental points lying outside the 95% parameter-propagated interval. Stoichiometric MFA linked the Medium C phenotype to increased amino acid catabolism, identified the intracellular sources for glutamate and lactate production, and enabled estimation of two new rate-constants for their production directly from stoichiometric flux, rather than fitted to data. MFA-guided repair reduced glutamate and lactate NRMSE in Medium C by 64% and 36%, respectively. The workflow provides a systematic strategy for improving model identifiability and using MFA to diagnose and repair structural discrepancies.

papers.title: Network-guided identification of candidate biomarkers for COPD-associated comorbidities using deep learning and real-world transcriptomic data
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) frequently coexists with infections, metabolic disease, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory lung injury and lung cancer. Molecular markers derived by comparing a comorbidity with healthy controls need not identify the transition from an established COPD state to that comorbidity. We therefore developed a two-stage computational strategy that asks a narrower question: which proteins can distinguish COPD samples from samples annotated with a specific COPD-associated comorbidity? First, a Human Protein Network (HPN; 17,302 proteins and 492,195 relationships) was encoded by 20 graph-derived features. A convolutional-neural-network ensemble, termed the functional-distance model (FDM), was trained on known drug-target-indication relationships. Stored training-set predictions yielded an apparent balanced accuracy of 0.811 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.627; these values describe resubstitution performance and are not an independent estimate of generalization. The COPD-centred network search evaluated 2,645 nearby proteins and retained 224 candidates using a COPD FDM score above 0.50. Candidate expression was then tested in independently assembled public patient-derived transcriptomic data using simple one-feature classifiers and cross-validation. The resulting exploratory panel contained GTF2I for bacterial infection, UBXN7 for type 2 diabetes, LIFR for hypertension, SRGN for lung neoplasm and FGF4 for pneumonitis. Across the saved cross-validation predictions, balanced accuracy ranged from 0.838 to 0.970 and MCC from 0.726 to 0.941. SRGN has direct experimental support in non-small-cell lung cancer, whereas the remaining candidates have varying indirect mechanistic support and should be regarded as hypotheses rather than established disease biomarkers. This work demonstrates an orthogonal discovery framework in which network-based functional prioritization and patient-derived molecular discrimination constrain one another. Its main contribution is methodological: it provides a reusable strategy for generating comorbidity-specific biomarker hypotheses from an index-disease state. Prospective longitudinal cohorts are required before claims of progression prediction or clinical utility can be made.

papers.title: Stream and lake network position structures freshwater microbial communities across multiple catchments
papers.abstract: Streams and lakes form hydrologically connected freshwater networks. Different environmental conditions and dispersal dynamics along the stream to lake continuum potentially affect bacterial community composition, although the strength of such effects may vary among individual catchments. Here, we analysed 224 water samples from 58 streams draining into eight lakes across Switzerland, covering the full continuum from headwaters to lake outlets. Bacterial community composition analyzed via 16S metabarcoding differed between streams and lakes, with a sharp turnover at stream and lake confluence, and this pattern was repeatable across all catchments. Lake communities had lower alpha diversity and lower overall beta dispersion than stream communities, despite hydrological connectivity with a diverse stream microbiome. Community composition in both lakes and streams differed between catchments, but this pattern was more pronounced in lakes. Lake communities were dominated by a small set of widespread and abundant core taxa, primarily established pelagic freshwater genera, that captured the catchment-level differences through shifts in relative abundance. In contrast, stream communities contained a comparatively less abundant core microbiome dominated by soil- and groundwater-associated genera, together with a larger and more diverse peripheral microbiome. Together, these findings show that bacterial community composition changes repeatably across the different positions of hydrological networks.

papers.title: CyranoPS, a novel compact temperate corynephage infecting Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001
papers.abstract: Here, we describe CyranoPS, a temperate phage isolated from the river Yvette in France, using the prophage-free strain Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001. Negative-stain electron microscopy revealed virions with siphovirus morphology. Its 14,910-bp genome has a GC content of 53.0% and 14-nt 3' overhangs at both ends. It carries 26 predicted genes, 10 without predicted functions, and no tRNAs. CyranoPS belongs to the newly established actinophage cluster ER, whose members have the smallest known genomes among Corynebacterium-infecting phages. Deletion of genes encoding the porin PorAH and the protein mycoloyltransferase MytC abolished infection, while genes encoding the mycomembrane proteins PorBC and ProtX were dispensable. CyranoPS established lysogeny in C. glutamicum through chromosomal integration probably mediated by its predicted tyrosine integrase. Integration truncated the immunity repressor gene Cyr_18, resulting in a protein devoid of its 15 C-terminal residues. The truncated repressor conferred stronger protection against superinfection than the full-length repressor. CyranoPS lysogens exhibited high levels of spontaneous prophage induction, reaching 109 PFU/mL under standard conditions, with no further increase upon treatment with mitomycin C. These findings suggest a potentially SOS-independent lytic-lysogenic switch and establish CyranoPS as a compact model to study infection and lysogeny regulation in Mycobacteriales.
